extraction.agency_name: Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission
extraction.parent_department: Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission

findings.title: Prince George’s County Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) lacked formal written policies and procedures for capital project management.
findings.description: DPR had not developed formal written policies and procedures governing its capital planning and project management operations. Staff were not provided with comprehensive formal guidance for planning projects, monitoring construction, or documenting oversight activities.
findings.recommendation: DPR should develop and implement formal written policies and procedures for capital planning and project management, including roles and responsibilities; establish performance expectations and reporting mechanisms to monitor effectiveness.

findings.title: The annual Capital Improvement Program documents did not contain certain project information to promote clarity and transparency, and may not have met a certain statutory requirement.
findings.description: CIP documents lacked specific project information needed for clarity and transparency, potentially failing a statutory requirement regarding construction schedules. Combining multiple projects under single Project Description Forms obscured funding details and made monitoring difficult.

dollar_amounts.context: expenditures for the 5 projects we originally selected
approved funding levels as of June 10, 2016

findings.recommendation: M-NCPPC - Prince George’s County should ensure its CIP includes supplementary information to identify individual projects and related funding; detailed project descriptions; and construction schedules that meet State law requirements.

findings.title: DPR had not established a comprehensive approach to documenting project activities and costs, including the retention of necessary project and contract documents.
findings.description: DPR had no formal guidance for staff regarding maintaining key project information or using its project management system. Staff did not fully use the system to monitor activities or retain documents electronically, precluding effective monitoring by management.
findings.recommendation: DPR should fully utilize the project management software system to establish timelines and monitor progress; develop a system user manual; and use form building capabilities to standardize information gathering.

findings.title: The duration of five projects tested was long, ranging from 7 years to 12 years. According to DPR, there were lengthy periods where Park Planning and Development (PPD) staff levels did not keep pace with increases in its CIP; however, DPR had not developed workload standards to identify staff resource needs.
findings.description: Five tested projects had long durations from substantial funding to completion ranging from 6.8 years to 12 years. DPR attributed delays to staffing limitations but lacked workload standards to assess resource needs or manage fluctuations in project activity.

dollar_amounts.context: combined construction contractor payments for the five projects tested
expenditures for contractors with design excess time

findings.recommendation: DPR should develop staffing workload standards to determine necessary resources for administering and overseeing projects and use this information for strategic planning.

findings.title: Site inspection results were not routinely recorded in the project management system and, for one project, the inspection documentation was not consistently prepared during the entire construction phase.
findings.description: Inspection results for four projects tested were not routinely recorded in the system, and documentation was not consistently prepared for one project. This lack of central recording hindered document security and monitoring of contractor performance.
findings.recommendation: DPR should specify in policies the desired frequency of site inspections; information to be recorded for each inspection; method for retaining results; and process for supervisory review.

findings.title: Many contract change orders did not appear to have been approved in a timely manner. DPR also did not consistently prepare documentation of its assessment of contractor proposed change order cost increases or extensions of time for work performance.
findings.description: Change orders were often not approved timely, with an average approval time of 46 days and some occurring after contract time periods expired. DPR failed to consistently document verification of the reasonableness of proposed cost increases or time extensions.

dollar_amounts.context: total value of 74 change orders processed
value of 32 significant change orders reviewed in detail
value of change orders approved within 14 days
value of remaining change orders taking longer to approve
value of proposed change order costs not verified by DPR

findings.recommendation: DPR should describe steps for reviewing change proposals and documentation required; determine targeted timeframe for obtaining final approvals considering approval levels.

findings.title: Contractors frequently did not complete their work within the timeframes specified in their contracts and DPR actions to hold contractors accountable were not always evident.
findings.description: Contractors frequently exceeded contract timeframes for completion, and DPR's actions to hold them accountable (e.g., liquidated damages) were not always evident. There were no formal guidelines on progressive steps to address untimely contractor performance.

dollar_amounts.context: expenditures for five contractors with design excess time

findings.recommendation: DPR should develop formal guidelines regarding progressive steps to address untimely contractor work performance; assess liquidated damages or document why assessment is not appropriate.

extraction.agency_response_summary: DPR agreed with all seven findings and recommendations. The agency acknowledged the lengthy time to complete some projects but noted that most time is spent before construction begins. DPR plans to implement policy changes, workload standards, and enhanced documentation processes within 12 to 18 months or by the end of 2018.
